rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Poisson's ratio σ = −(lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain) is a dimensionless material constant between 0 and 0.5 describing how a body thins when stretched. It links the elastic moduli through E = 2G(1+σ) = 3B(1−2σ). σ = 0.5 corresponds to an incompressible material, while cork (σ ≈ 0) barely changes width.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Poisson's ratio: σ = −(lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain)
Relation with moduli: E = 2G(1 + σ); E = 3B(1 − 2σ)
σ from E and B: σ = (3B − E)/(6B)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Definition and Sign Convention:** $\sigma = -( ext{lateral strain})/( ext{longitudinal strain})$. The negative sign makes $\sigma$ positive for ordinary materials (lateral and longitudinal strains have opposite signs). The ratio is dimensionless — dividing one dimensionless strain by another.  ·  **Volume Change Constraint:** The fractional volume change under uniaxial stress is $\Delta V/V = \varepsilon(1 - 2\sigma)$. For $\sigma = 0.5$ (incompressible), $\Delta V/V = 0$ — volume is conserved. For $\sigma < 0.5$, volume increases slightly during stretching.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Remember the minus sign in σ = −(lateral)/(longitudinal) — it makes typical σ positive.  ·  σ is dimensionless — do not attach units.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Wire: L = 2 m, d = 1 mm, ΔL = 2 mm, σ = 0.3 → diameter change = σ × ε × d = 0.3×10⁻³×1 = 3×10⁻⁴ mm.  ·  From moduli: E = 2×10¹¹, G = 8×10¹⁰ → σ = E/(2G) − 1 = 1.25 − 1 = 0.25.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'Poisson's ratio has units of strain.' ✅ It is a RATIO of two strains — dimensionless.  ·  ❌ 'Poisson's ratio can be greater than 1.' ✅ No — the thermodynamic limit is 0.5 for isotropic materials (a few exotic anisotropic materials exceed 0.5 but never 1).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Compute σ from measured lateral and longitudinal strains.  ·  Compute σ from E and G using E = 2G(1+σ).

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: σ is dimensionless — any answer with units is automatically wrong.  ·  From E and G: σ = E/(2G) − 1 — do this division first, then subtract 1.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: A wire of diameter 1 mm is stretched so its length increases by 0.5%. The diameter reduces by 0.15%. Find Poisson's ratio.  ·  Steel has E = 2×10¹¹ N/m² and B = 1.6×10¹¹ N/m². Find σ from E = 3B(1−2σ).

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Definitions and limits of Poisson's ratio are a standard short-answer.  ·  Computing σ from E and G (or E and B) is a common numerical.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Poisson's ratio σ = −(lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain) is dimensionless.  ·  Typical range for isotropic materials: 0 < σ < 0.5.  ·  σ connects the elastic moduli: E = 2G(1+σ) = 3B(1−2σ).  ·  σ = 0.5 → incompressible; σ = 0 → no lateral deformation.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Poisson's ratio is the (negative) ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain — always dimensionless.  ·  σ typically lies between 0 and 0.5 for isotropic materials.  ·  σ links E, B and G: E = 2G(1+σ) = 3B(1−2σ).  ·  σ = 0.5 means incompressible (volume is conserved); σ = 0 means no lateral change (cork).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Poisson's ratio is named after Siméon Denis Poisson (1829) who derived it theoretically for isotropic materials.  ·  The majority of materials have σ between 0.25 and 0.35 — metals cluster around 0.3.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: A rubber cord (σ = 0.5) is stretched. Show that its volume stays constant.  ·  Find the lateral strain on a 2 mm square bar stretched with longitudinal strain 10⁻³ (σ = 0.3).  ·  A concrete block (σ = 0.2) is compressed by 0.1%. Find the lateral expansion.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Conceptual: why cork for bottle stoppers → σ ≈ 0.  ·  Volume change ΔV/V = ε(1 − 2σ) appears in numerical questions.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Lateral strain: ε_long = 2×10⁻³, σ = 0.25 → ε_lat = −5×10⁻⁴.  ·  Volume: ε = 10⁻³, σ = 0.3 → ΔV/V = 10⁻³(1−0.6) = 4×10⁻⁴.

rows.text: Poisson's ratio is the ratio of lateral strain to: → B  ·  Poisson's ratio for an incompressible material is: → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Poisson's ratio (σ):** when a body is stretched (or compressed), it becomes thinner (or thicker) in the perpendicular directions. Poisson's ratio is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain: σ = −(lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain) = −(β/α). The minus sign keeps σ positive because lateral strain is opposite in sign to longitudinal strain.  ·  **Why it is dimensionless:** Poisson's ratio divides one strain by another — strain is dimensionless, so σ has no units and no dimensions. Its value for most materials lies between 0 and 0.5.  ·  **Typical values:** cork ≈ 0 (no lateral change), concrete ≈ 0.1–0.2, steel ≈ 0.25–0.3, copper ≈ 0.33, aluminium ≈ 0.34, rubber ≈ 0.5 (nearly incompressible). A hypothetical material with σ = 0.5 would conserve volume exactly.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ΔV/V = ε(1 − 2σ) describes volume change on stretching.  ·  σ from E and G: σ = E/(2G) − 1  ·  Fractional volume change: ΔV/V = ε(1 − 2σ)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Material State Limits:** The thermodynamic bounds are $-1 < \sigma < 0.5$ for isotropic materials. Most common materials have $0 < \sigma < 0.5$. Auxetic materials (negative $\sigma$) expand laterally when stretched — rare and engineered. Fluids have no defined Poisson's ratio (no shear rigidity).  ·  ΔV/V = ε(1 − 2σ) — volume change during stretching depends only on σ and strain.  ·  ❌ 'Lateral strain equals longitudinal strain.' ✅ Lateral strain = −σ × longitudinal strain, with σ typically between 0 and 0.5.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'When stretched, volume always increases.' ✅ If σ = 0.5 the volume is constant; for σ < 0.5 the volume increases slightly (ΔV/V = ε(1−2σ)).  ·  ❌ 'Cork and rubber have similar σ.' ✅ Cork ≈ 0, rubber ≈ 0.5 — at opposite ends of the range.  ·  ❌ 'Poisson's ratio is a force.' ✅ It is a pure, dimensionless ratio of deformation (strain) — not a force or modulus.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Cork: σ ≈ 0 → bottle stopper keeps its width when squeezed.  ·  For steel, σ ≈ 0.25–0.3; for rubber, σ ≈ 0.5; for cork, σ ≈ 0.  ·  Volume is conserved when σ = 0.5 (ΔV/V = 0).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB often asks to compute σ using E = 2G(1+σ) given E and G.  ·  σ = −(lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain) — always dimensionless, always use the negative ratio.  ·  σ links E, B, G: E = 2G(1+σ) and E = 3B(1−2σ).
